en: The Theravāda Vinaya:
Bhikkhunī Vibhaṅga,
Nissaggiya Section (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on the Set of Six:
The Training Rule on Having Something Bartered for One’s Own Use.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the bhikkhunī Thullanandā was learned, an eloquent speaker, confident, and skilled in delivering a discourse on the Dhamma.
Many people waited upon the bhikkhunī Thullanandā.
At that time, the courtyard of the bhikkhunī Thullanandā’s dwelling was falling into ruin.
People said this to the bhikkhunī Thullanandā:
“Venerable lady, why is this courtyard of yours leaking?
“Friends, there are no donors; there are no builders,” she replied.
Then those people, having collected contributions for the purpose of a courtyard for the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, gave the requisites to the bhikkhunī Thullanandā.
But with those requisites, the bhikkhunī Thullanandā herself also made requests and had medicine purchased, which she then consumed.
When the people found out, they were indignant, disparaged her, and complained:

“How could the noble lady Thullanandā indeed exchange one thing for another by means of requisites that were intended for another purpose, designated for another, personal, and obtained through solicitation? … [The Buddha asked:

“Is it true, monks, that the nun Thullanandā exchanges one thing for another by means of requisites that were intended for another purpose, designated for another, personal, and obtained through solicitation? [They replied:
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:

“… How indeed, monks, can the bhikkhunī Thullanandā exchange one thing for another by means of a requisite that was requested for her own private use, intended for a specific purpose, and obtained through solicitation?
This, monks, is neither for the inspiration of those without faith nor for the increase of the faith of those who have it…” [and so on].
And furthermore, monks, the bhikkhunīs should recite this training rule thus:

“Whichever bhikkhunī, having requested a personal requisite that was intended for another purpose and designated for another, should exchange it for something else, there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya). Whichever bhikkhunī...
[as above]... means:
Whichever [nun] of such a kind... "a nun" ...pe...
this is the nun intended in this context.
"By means of a requisite intended for another purpose" means:
given for the sake of something else. "Belonging to an individual" means: [given] for the sake of a specific person.
By one single bhikkhunī, not by the Saṅgha, nor by a group.
"Having asked for it herself" means having requested it personally.
"Should she exchange for something else":
setting aside that which was given for a specific purpose, if she exchanges it for something else, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in the act of undertaking;
with the acquisition [of the item], it becomes an offense entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).
It must be relinquished either to the Saṅgha, or to a group, or to a single bhikkhunī.
And this, monks, is how it should be relinquished:
…pe…

“Venerable ladies, this other thing that I have had exchanged for a personal requisite intended for another purpose and obtained by means of a request is to be relinquished; I relinquish it to the Saṅgha.
…pe… “Let her give it,” …pe… “Let them give it,” …pe…
“I give it to the noble lady.
If she exchanges something else for what was intended for another purpose while perceiving it as being for another purpose, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If she exchanges something else for what was intended for another purpose while being in doubt, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If she exchanges something for something else when it is not for that purpose, thinking it is not for that purpose, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
Having forfeited it, it must be restored to the person from whom it was received.
If she exchanges something for something else when it is not for that purpose, thinking it is for that purpose, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is not for another’s purpose, but she is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is not for another’s purpose, and she perceives it as not being for another’s purpose, there is no offense.
There is no offense—
He offers the remainder;
he offers it after having informed the owners;
in times of emergency.
"Against one who is insane," "against one who is a first-offender.
The tenth training rule is concluded.
